planting.note: Plant divisions or dormant crowns in fall into humus-rich, evenly moist soil under high shade; established clumps tolerate dry shade and root competition from trees once settled.

directions: This gold-leaved sport of the thuggish Black Sea comfrey relative emerges in late winter with rough, hand-sized leaves that open brilliant chartreuse-gold before settling to a softer lime tone as the canopy above fills in. Branching spikes of small, reflexed blue borage-type flowers rise above the foliage in late winter to early spring, well ahead of most companion perennials, and draw early bumblebees. Give it the same dry-shade, root-filled ground that defeats the plain green species and it will knit into a dense weed-suppressing patch, though the bright color is strongest with a little morning sun and fades in deeper shade. Cut tattered summer foliage back hard after bloom to force a fresh, cleaner-colored flush.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden catalog

planting.note: Divide and transplant in fall or very early spring while dormant, siting in moist, organically rich shaded ground; spreads by rhizome so allow room or edge the patch.

directions: A New Zealand selection prized for coarse, bristly-textured leaves that unfurl bright gold in earliest spring before gradually greening as summer heat builds. Wiry pink flower stems carry sprays of small starry blue flowers held just above the emerging foliage in late winter, a nectar source for the first bumblebees out of hibernation and, in milder gardens, overwintering hummingbirds. Like the species it runs by thick rhizomes into an efficient groundcover for the driest, most root-bound shade under mature trees, so it is best used where its vigor is an asset rather than a liability. The gold spring color is most pronounced with a few hours of filtered or morning sun.

planting.note: Set divisions into humus-rich, reliably moist but well-drained woodland soil in fall; this selection tolerates colder winters than most cappadocica forms, so mulch is optional once established.

directions: Selected and named for its unusually cold-hardy constitution, this cultivar carries sprays of soft, light-blue, forget-me-not flowers over mounds of grey-green, slightly fuzzy foliage in mid-spring. The muted leaf color reads cooler and more silvery than the plain species, giving the clump a gentler presence among ferns and hellebores. It forms a tight, non-spreading rosette rather than running, making it a reliable long-term edger for a shaded border where other cappadocica selections sometimes struggle through harsher winters. Light summer shade and steady moisture keep the foliage from scorching after bloom.

planting.note: Plant in fall into evenly moist, humus-rich soil in light shade; deadheading spent sprays through summer encourages the extended repeat bloom this cultivar is grown for.

directions: Unlike most navelworts, which flower in one spring flush, this introduction keeps producing its small sky-blue, white-eyed flowers over sea-green, lance-shaped foliage from spring clear through summer whenever moisture is adequate. The low, dense clumps stay tidy without spreading aggressively, so it pairs well with hostas and epimediums as a long-blooming groundlevel accent rather than a running mat. Performance is best in cool, lightly shaded sites with consistent soil moisture; prolonged heat and dry spells shorten the bloom window. A light haircut after the first flush can refresh the mound and prompt further flowering into fall.
sources: Walters Gardens / Dutch breeder catalog listings

planting.note: Plant pips or divisions in fall just below the soil surface in moist, humus-rich shaded ground; variegation holds best with some filtered light rather than deep shade.

directions: This German selection carries the familiar paired, broadly ovate leaves of lily-of-the-valley but edged in an irregular creamy-yellow margin that stays legible through the growing season rather than fading to plain green by midsummer. Short arching stems carry the usual fragrant, pendent white bells in late spring, nestled among the variegated foliage. It spreads by rhizome at the same vigorous pace as the species, so it is best used as a running groundcover under deciduous shrubs or along a shaded path edge where its colonizing habit and bright leaf margin are both put to use. Division every few years keeps the patch from crowding out slower neighbors.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil; this white-flowered variety needs the same cool, evenly damp site as the pink-flowered species.

directions: This pale-flowered botanical variety departs from the typical rose-pink Heloniopsis in carrying short, fringed clusters of white flowers above a compact rosette of leathery, strap-shaped evergreen leaves in early spring. The low buns slowly offset into small colonies rather than running, making them well suited to a damp, shaded rock garden pocket or streamside planting alongside other Asian woodland rarities. It shares the species' intolerance of summer drought and benefits from a steady seep or regularly watered site rather than typical border conditions. Remove faded flower stalks after seed set to keep the evergreen rosettes looking tidy through winter.
sources: The Hardy Plant Society (UK) journal notes

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, gritty, humus-rich woodland soil with reliable drainage; this compact variety is slower to establish than the typical species and resents standing water.

directions: This miniature Japanese collector's variety forms tight, evergreen four-inch buns of narrow leaves, far smaller and slower to spread than the typical species, with taller flower stalks rising above the foliage in early spring to carry whorls of flaring, tubular white flowers punctuated by dark purple stamens. Fall color on the stiff foliage turns a soft apricot-orange, adding interest well after bloom. Its diminutive size suits a shaded trough, raised woodland bed, or alpine-style planting where larger companions would overwhelm it, and it wants consistent moisture without ever sitting wet. Bees readily visit the spring flowers in sheltered sites.

planting.note: Divide and move clumps only while dormant in very early spring, into consistently moist, neutral-to-alkaline, humus-rich woodland soil in dappled shade; variegated patterning can be unstable and some divisions revert to plain foliage.

directions: This selection of the Asian twinleaf carries the same rounded, two-lobed leaflets as the species but mottled with irregular white spotting that emerges alongside the earliest growth, fading somewhat as the rounded leaves mature through the season. Solitary violet-blue, cup-shaped flowers open low to the ground in earliest spring before the patterned leaves fully expand, a brief but choice display for a shaded rock garden or woodland trough. Because the spotting can be genetically unstable, plants are propagated only by division of confirmed clones rather than seed, and any all-green offsets should be removed to keep the patch true. Site it where it will not be disturbed once established, as twinleaf resents transplanting once mature.
